MERIDIAN, MISS.
Meridian, Miss., August 1.—(Special.) The criminal terms of the Lauderdale county circuit court to be convened in Meridian tomorrow by Judge C. C. Miller, in all probability will be one of the most interesting in many years because of the number and character of some of the crimes.

It will be the first term to be held by Judge Miller, who was appointed by Governor Russell to preside until a special election can be held to elect a successor for the full term of Judge Rowland Heidelberg, resigned. Judge Miller is one of Meridian's foremost lawyers, son of the late C. C. Miller, who was a leading lawyer of the state As he is a candidate for the full term his conduct of the court will be filled with interest and watched eagerly by his friends and supporters.

It will become his duty to deliver a charge to the grand jury for investigation of crime in this county and included in those to be probed are three of the foulest murders ever committed in this section of the state, one lynching and two attempted lynchings that have occurred since the last session of the criminal court in February.

The murders to receive the attention of the grand jury are those of James A. Tyral, suburban merchant, who was shot and fatally wounded in his store. On the same night the murder of Henry W. Davis, aged night watchman at a local lumber plant, was shot to death and robbed. For the commission of these crimes two negroes, Henry Llovd and Will Echols, were arrested and taken to Jackson, where they have been held in jail for fear that they might be lynched. One of the negroes, since arrest, the officers say, has confessed, implicating the other. The next murder to horrify the county was that of Miss Carrie Hatcher, eighteen-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George W. Hatcher, who was mysteriously choked to death near her home and her body thrown into a small brook.

The grand jury is also to probe the lynching of James Spencer, negro postal clerk, following his attack on Otto Parker, white postal clerk, while the two were on duty in the same car; the attempted lynching of Percy Thompson, for attempted criminal assault on a young Syrian girl, and the attempted lynching of Ludie Martin, arrested as a suspect in the Hatcher murder case. There are also a number of other criminal cases to receive attention, such as burglary and robbery.
james-spencer-basic-city.A2:
GRAND JURY TOLD
TO GO AFTER MOB
New Circuit Judge Delivers Ringing Charge When Jury Is Sworn In
Meridian. Miss., August 2.—(Special.)—Circuit Judge C. C. Miller, assuming the bench for the first time today following his appointment by Governor Russell to succeed to the vacancy caused by the resignation of Judge Rowland W. Heidelberg, delivered a ringing charge to the grand jury when that body was sworn in after opening the criminal term of the Lauderdale county circuit court. He charged the jury specially with reference to the recent lynching of James Spencer, negro postal clerk, by a small party of masked men when the prisoner was being taken to Enterprise, in Clarke county, to answer to a charge of assault with intent on Otho Parker, white postal clerk, while the two were at work in their car as it passed through that county. He also called the jury's special attention to recent attempts by mobs of unmasked white men to force the county jail here in an effort to get possession of Percy Thompson, negro, charged with attempted criminal assault on a young Syrian girl, and Ludie Martin, arrested as a suspect in connection with the murder of Miss Carrie Hatcher, 18-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George W. Hatcher, prosperous planter residing a few miles from Meridian, the girl having been choked to death and her body cast by the murderers into a brook in a pasture near the Hatcher home. Judge Miller, in referring to the reckless disregard of the law by mobs, asked the jury to exert every effort to bring the guilty parties to justice, and he would see that the law is vindicated. With W. T. Rainey, planter, as foreman, the remaining members of the grand jury are as follows: H. E. Curtis, L. E. Cobb, R. S. Kinard, Amos Brunson, J. L. Welch, I. P. Vincent, D. L. Little, J. W. james-spencer-basic-city.A4:
BUSY SESSION AHEAD FOR COURT AT MERIDIAN
MERIDIAN, Miss., Aug. 4. (Spl.) — Circuit Judge C. C. Miller convened the criminal term of circuit court Monday, empaneling and charging the grand jury and getting ready for the grind that is to follow in the next four weeks.

Among the investigations to be made by the grand jury are three murders, one lynching and two attempted lynchings. Henry Lloyd and Will Echols, both negroes, are held for the murder of James A. Tyrell, a suburban merchant, and the same two are charged with the murder of H. W. Davis, a night watchman.

An investigation will be made into the death of Miss Carrie Hatcher, the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Geo. W. Hatcher, of Marion, whose dead body was found in a swamp bearing marks of violence. Her death remains a mystery.

A probe will also be made into the lynching of James Spencer, a negro railway postal clerk, who was shot to death by masked men near Basic City, while he was in charge of an officer en route to Clarke county to answer to a charge of assault with a knife on Otho Parker, another mail clerk, the fight taking place in the mail car of the train while passing through Clarke county.
james-spencer-basic-city.A5:
LAUDERDALE COUNTY GRAND JURY Highly Praises Judge C. C. Miller.
The grand jury made its final report to Judge C. C. Miller late yesterday and was discharged. Along with the final report, the body returned 14 indictments, making a total of 33 for the eight days in session, one of the best records ever made by a Lauderdale county grand jury. The body also takes occasion in its report to commend the work of judge Miller in presiding over the court along with other court officials, all of whom have done their utmost to carry out the announced policy of the judge that the business of the court shall be expedited in every way possible to lessen the expense.

One or two minor cases were disposed of this morning after which the trial of Fannie Walker, indicted for the murder of her husband, Richard Walker. about a year ago was taken up. The jury was quickly empaneled and a number of witnesses were examined before the noon adjournment. The case will go to the jury and a verdict is expected during the late afternoon.

The report of the grand jury as submitted by W. T. Rainey is as follows: "To the Hon. C. C. Miller, judge of the Circuit court 10th. Judicial district of Miss. "We the grand jury empanelled and sworn for the August term 1920. of the criminal court of Lauderdale county after being in session eight days, beg to make this our final report:

"We have examined 177 witnesses, and returned 33 true bills.
We had summoned and brought before us a great many witnesses in connection with the foul murder of Miss Carrie Hatcher and as much as each and every member of this body deplores the fact we have been unable to discover any evidence what ever that tends to show the perpetrator of this crime.

We desire to thank all of the county officials who have rendered their assistance in any way during our deliberations. We desire to express our disapproval of mob violence that has been perpetrated in the county by irresponsible persons. We made investigation with reference to these mobs and were unable to obtain evidence sufficient to find indictments. We commend the sheriff and his deputies, also the assistance rendered by the chief of police and his department, for their prompt action in quelling disturbances which may have had a serious result if not promptly and properly handled.

"We also desire to commend Your Honor for the able and expedient manner in which you have dispatched the business of this your first term of court. We call attention to the fact that during the first week of the term two homicide cases were tried for dastardly and cowardly assassination of our citizens and the death penalty assessed in both instances and you have shown that delay in the enforcement of the laws will not be tolerated. By your activity in the dispatch of business you have shortened the term of this court and reduced the expenses incident to a long term.

"Having fully reported we ask to be discharged."

lige-daniels-center-1920-08-02.A7:
NEGRO LYNCHED IN COURTHOUSE YARD
Lynching Follows Announcement of Confession of Murder of Woman
By Associated Press

Center, Tex., August 2.—Lige Daniels, a negro, charged with the murder of Mrs. Maggie Hall, was taken from the county jail here late today by a mob of over a thousand men and lynched to a tree in the courthouse yard. The mob wrecked the steel cell to get at the negro.

The lynching followed announcement by officers of a full confession made to the grand jury now in session and also to the district attorney, it was said.

Unconscious, with her skull crushed and her body bruised and lacerated, Mrs. Hall, the wife of a well-known farmer living near Center, was found at a lonely spot last Thursday night. She was brought here for medical attention, but died Friday.

Capt. W. A. Bridges, commanding Company L, Seventh cavalry, received wire instructions from Austin to protect the negro and prevent the lynching, but he was unable to find any of the members of his company in time for mobilization.

The crowd dispersed after the lynching and the town resumed its normal appearance.

Gulf State Adds Victim to Score of Mob Injustice
SHREVEPORT, LA., Aug. 2.—Lige Daniels, colored, was lynched this afternoon by a mob, and hanged right in the Court House Square at Center, Texas. Daniels had been charged with the murder of Mrs. Maggie Hall, and as customary down in this section, the mob, to justify its defiance of law, announced their victim had "confessed" to the crime.

The mob did not wait for the shades of night" as the time to perpetrate the taking of life without hearing or trial, but boldly went about its work in the early afternoon—in the broad day light when all could see and enjoy its canabalistic rights.

Although the lynching was done in broad day—the members of the mob not even resorting to masks to disguise themselves, the usual Southern coroner's verdict—"Died at the hands of unknown parties" will close the incident. This lynching, as recent previous ones have done, will only serve to increase the hegira of Colored people from the South to the North to escape the rule of lynching mobs.

SHERIFF GIVES JAIL KEYS TO MOB
Center, Texas, Aug. 11—Lige Daniels, accused of having murdered a white woman, was taken from the county jail by a mob of "representative citizens" and lynched in the courthouse yard, here last week. The lynching followed the usual statement given out by the officers that they had obtained a full confession of guilt from the defendant. The keys to the steel cage in which Daniels was held are said to have been turned over to leaders of the lynching party by the sheriff.

Soldiers Said To Be Among Lynchers
Capt. W. A. Bridges, commanding officer of L Troop 7 Cavalry, received instructions from the governor at Austin to prevent the lynching. It is alleged, however, that the captain was unable to mobilize his troop because most of them were participants in the lynching.

SAYS TEXAS GOVERNMENT COMPLETELY BREAKS DOWN
Today the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, with headquarters at 70 Fifth avenue, New York, released a copy of a telegram just sent to Governor W. P. Hobby, of Texas, with reference to the lynching on August 2 of a Negro at Center, Tex. The association's telegram calls attention to the fact that when two Negroes were lynched by a mob on July 6, Governor Hobby declared that Texas could handle its own affairs without outside interference. Although evidence showed later that both of the Negroes were innocent of the crime with which they were charged, the State of Texas made no arrests and secured no indictments of any of the lynchers.

The association calls attention to the fact that the lynching on Monday night was the eighth in Texas since January 1. James W. Johnson, field secretary of the association, who signed the telegram, declared that Texas government had completely broken down when State troops, when ordered to protect the prisoner/ could not be located by the officers in time to prevent the lynching. Mr. Johnson declared that since Texas had failed, the Federal Government must sooner or later intervene to protect the lives of American citizens.

How Arthur Boys Were Lynched And Three Young Sisters Raped Hitherto Unpublished Facts About Mob Outrage at Paris, Texas, July 6-Officer of the Law Assaults Innocent Girls
The following letter has been sent out by James Weldon Johnson, acting secretary of the N. A. A. C. P., giving hitherto unpublished facts in connection with the lynching of the Arthur boys at Paris, Texas, on July 6, and the subsequent outraging of their three young sisters, aged 20, 17 and 14, by officers of the law and twenty other white men. Mr. Johnson's letter includes a letter from a citizen of Paris, whose identity is naturally withheld from publication.

Sisters Raped By Twenty White Men
Inside Facts About Lynching in Paris, Texas, Told by a Letter to National Association.

BROTHERS LYNCHED

Bodies Burned and Dragged Through Streets of Colored Section.

New York, Sept. 2—The inside story of the lynching of Irving and Herman Arthur aged 19 and 22 years respectively is told for the first time by the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People in a letter received from a colored witness.

The Auturm boys worked a farm on halves for a white man named Hedges. The latter missed that the boys work six full days a week, and worked Saturday afternoon, and packed up their belongings to move Hedges and the boys snap back and killed both vultures.

A posse of white men was formed and lynched both brothers afterwards wagging their bodies near the streets of the town yelling: "There are the barbedwren Niggers, as you Niggers come out and see

"The three Arthur girls, aged 29, 17 and 14 were in jail on the pretence of protection. They were severely beaten for screaming while the mob was taking their brothers from jail. Later on in the night they were taken to the police and there as they were given a bounty of molasses, a small sack of flour and some bread and told to eat the road.

"I forgot to mention that these girls were stripped of all their clothing in the basement and they were certainly assaulted by the officers and then by 20 other white men of the same low type. They were threatened with death if they ever told it, then they were made to leave town by these same officers. Hundreds of Negroes have left Paris since this occurrence and many have been planning to leave as soon as possible. You are at liberty to publish what you see fit of this only keep secret my name."

THEY DARED TO PROTECT THEIR OWN
The letter sent to the National Association for Advancement of Colored People by a Paris, Texas, citizen, detailing the lynching of two young Colored men—brothers, which we published in last week's issue of The Advocate, was distressing—it was shocking.

One of the victims had spent eighteen months on the firing line in France—fighting for world democracy. Because the two men resented the insult given to their three sisters, they were lynched, the charred remains being dragged through the streets behind a truck, in imitation of the customs of a far-off age when brutish emperors dragged the lifeless bodies of their victims behind their chariots.

And yet these United States talk much about interfering with the right of self-determination by other countries.

And yet these United States, who willingly accepted this young Colored man to brave German shrapnel over in France, rebels against the atrocities committed by bolsheviki in Russia; complains against England's treatment of the Irish—sets itself up as a regulator of the morals and religions of the world.

Before the eyes of these two brothers who were lynched, their three sisters were stripped of their clothing; were thrown into jail; were criminally outraged by the officers and twenty other whites, and all, in the final analysis, because their brothers refused to work on a half holiday, on a farm on which they were employed as "half" tenants.

But not one of those men—those beasts who outraged the three sisters—was arrested. Not one of the men who lynched the two brothers who dared to protect their home and the virtue of their sisters, has been brought to justice!

And yet some folk prate about democracy in America.

UNSPEAKABLE BRUTALITY.
How the Arthur Boys Were Lynched and Three Sisters Outraged— "Southern Chivalry."

PARIS, Texas—I am writing you concerning a lynching which occurred here last month. Doubtless you have long since gotten the details, if not I will give you facts as I witnessed them. Herman and Irvin Arthur, Negroes with their parents were tenants on Hodges Farm. They were working on halves, a system whereby the landlord furnishes his tenants and at harvest time takes half the crop and the amount with interest which he furnished his tenants during the year. Against the usual custom here Hodges compelled his tenants to work all day Saturday. This they did for a time, washing and ironing their clothes on Sunday. When they refused to work longer than noon Saturday Hodges became angry and went to their home on the farm 3 days before the murder and took their dinner off the stove and threw it into the yard. He also kicked their stove and household goods out in the yard. During this time Hodges' son held a gun on the Negroes. He also compelled the boys to pull off their shoes and clothes; their sisters to pull off their dresses and give them to claim, the Negroes were in debt to him. After this they decided to move from his farm. When they had begun loading a truck Hodges and his son came up and began shooting at them. Herman Arthur ran into the house and secured a gun and came out and killed both men who were yet firing at them. A mob lynched both Negroes. After they were burned their bodies were dragged thru the streets on which colored people lived. There was a regular parade of 17 cars and a truck with white men crying aloud—"Here are the barbecued niggers; all you niggers come out and see them and take warning." When asked if they were sorry they killed the white man, Herman Arthur who had recently served 18 months on the firing line in France replied, "No, I am not sorry, I would do the same thing again. I would kill any man who imposed upon my mother and sisters.
